analysis.one_liner: Abolishes jury-awarded punitive damages in federal-law and interstate-commerce cases, replacing them with court-assessed fines.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee: introduced in October 1992 with no cosponsors, it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated punitive damages — the extra money juries can award to punish a company for reckless or malicious conduct — in any case arising under federal law or involving interstate commerce, which covers most injury and product-liability suits against large companies. In their place, a judge could impose a 'punitive fine,' but only after the injured person proved by a heightened standard of evidence that the company acted with actual malice — not merely negligence. Juries would largely lose their say over whether and how much punishment applies. The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when Congress adjourned.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations facing lawsuits — manufacturers, drug makers, insurers, and other large defendants — would gain the most. They would face far lower exposure to large unpredictable jury awards, would rarely be liable for an employee's misconduct unless top executives authorized or ratified it, and could split liability so each defendant pays only its own assessed share. Liability insurers would also benefit from more predictable, smaller payouts.

how_it_helps.text: It abolishes punitive damages entirely for covered claims and replaces them with a judge-assessed 'punitive fine,' so corporate defendants no longer face open-ended jury awards.

A punitive fine could only be imposed if the plaintiff proved malice by 'clear and convincing evidence' — a much higher bar than ordinary proof — and the bill states that no degree of negligence, even gross negligence, can meet that burden.

A company could not be fined for its employee's conduct unless a superior officer with policymaking authority authorized, participated in, or ratified it, shielding firms from punishment for front-line misconduct.

Any party could force a two-part trial in which the jury first decides compensation without hearing evidence about the defendant's outrageous conduct, and the judge — not the jury — sets the amount of any fine.
When multiple defendants are involved, each pays only the fine assessed against it individually, allocated by relative culpability, eliminating joint punitive liability.
The bill's sponsors argued that unpredictable punitive awards raise consumer prices, increase litigation costs, and reduce incentives for research and development.

analysis.who_pays: People seriously injured by corporate misconduct would bear the cost. Even a recklessly negligent company would face no punitive consequence unless the victim could prove actual malice or conscious indifference at a heightened evidentiary standard — often impossible without internal company documents. Injured people would also lose the leverage that punitive exposure gives them in settlement negotiations, and in many cases a judge rather than a jury would decide whether punishment applies at all.

drawbacks.text: The malice standard excludes punishment for gross negligence entirely, so a company whose conscious corner-cutting gravely injures people would face no punitive sanction unless the victim proved near-intentional indifference.
It shifts the decision about punishment from juries to judges in many cases, removing the community check on corporate conduct that punitive damages have historically provided.

Requiring a plaintiff to present a prima facie case for a punitive fine 30 days before trial, before full discovery of company records, could get the claim thrown out before the evidence needed to prove it is available.
The findings themselves concede that punishment and deterrence are the purpose of punitive damages; replacing them with a rarely-awarded fine weakens the deterrent signal to other companies.
It applies to claims made after enactment even if the underlying conduct occurred years earlier, changing the rules midstream for pending injuries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Businesses gain real predictability, and there is a good-faith argument that runaway awards raise prices and chill innovation. But the bill's design goes far beyond curbing outliers: it eliminates punishment for even gross negligence, moves the decision from juries to judges, and shields companies from responsibility for their employees' conduct. The main cost falls on people hurt by corporate misconduct, who would rarely be able to meet the heightened proof requirements. The scales clearly tilt toward defendants.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. John Danforth introduced the bill on October 6, 1992, near the end of the two-year session.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; no markup, committee vote, or floor action followed.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill was not carried over.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate defendants and liability insurers are better off: the punitive-damages exposure the bill targeted was never enacted into law, but the existing jury system — with its deterrent power for injured people — remained intact because the bill died. Status quo winners are therefore both defendants (no new limits) and the public (no limits imposed either); in the narrow sense that the bill failed, injured consumers avoided the restrictions it would have placed on their claims.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate defendants; the bill never advanced

for.name: Sen. John C. Danforth
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued the Senate's only action on it: reading it twice and referring it to committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup, committee vote, or report before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors and no votes or floor debate, the record shows no partisan pattern — only a single Republican sponsor and no legislative movement.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants (manufacturers, product makers, drug companies)
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated punitive damages in most cases against them, requiring victims to prove actual malice at a heightened standard and protecting companies from liability for employee misconduct unless executives ratified it. That gain comes directly at the expense of injured people's ability to punish and deter reckless corporate conduct.

Capping and routinizing punitive exposure makes payouts smaller and more predictable, directly reducing what insurers pay on injury claims. Their savings come from the same pool of money that compensates injured people.

industries.industry: Trial lawyers and plaintiff-side civil litigation
industries.note: Plaintiffs' attorneys would face a much harder path to punitive awards, longer bifurcated trials, and reduced settlement leverage. Their interest in this bill runs alongside their injured clients'.
